CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYIS OF MEASURE D

Measure D is a voter-sponsored initiative measure. If approved, Measure D would amend the Los
Altos (“City”) Municipal Code by adding a new Chapter 14.92 entitled “Downtown Parking Plazas.”
Measure D defines the Downtown Parking Plazas as the “publicly-accessible, open and surface
parking lots located in the Downtown area which are owned by the City.” They are commonly
known as Plazas | through 10.

The 2026 Ballot Measure Impact Analysis - 9212 Report (“9212 Report”) for Measure D found that
“’,. the Ballot Measure would potentially limit new development by adding additional constraints to
development on the City-owned Downtown Parking Plazas. Although there is an exception for
‘affordable housing’ on Plazas 7 and 8, it is not clear if mixed-income housing or other development
programs that include affordable housing could be approved without a subsequent Ballot Measure.
This would impact development of even affordable multifamily housing on all these lots, including
Plazas 7 and 8, by potentially complicating development opportunities. This would impact Program
1.H (‘Facilitation housing on City-owned sites’) and other Housing Element programs and policies.”

Unless approved by a majority vote of the City’s voters, Measure D would prohibit the City from
taking the following actions affecting the Parking Plazas: selling, leasing, or otherwise conveying
them; changing their use which would dimmish the availability of public parking; declaring them as
surplus land; constructing any capital project that permanently diminishes the availability of public
parking; modifying them by adding additional levels; modifying them in a way that would
negatively affect protected trees or tree canopy; or entering into a development agreement or similar
agreement that would allow a third-party to take action prohibited by it.

Measure D provides few actions to be taken without a majority vote of the City’s voters such as
maintaining and repairing the Parking Plazas and hosting the farmers’ market or similar short-term
events.

The processing, interpretation, and validity of Measure D would be governed by the Election Code
and state law. The 9212 Report found “If the Ballot Measure were to pass and then subsequently be
challenged in court, the City would be required to pay defense costs of the challenge and potentially
indemnify the proponents. The City would also be required to defend the Ballot Measure and any
implementation of the Ballot Measure, until ended by voters.” The 9212 Report attached the June
15, 2026, YIMBY Law letter that stated, “To dispel any potential ambiguity, we are prepared to sue
Los Altos the instant this measure is adopted.” Measure D’s defense costs would come from the

City’s General Fund.

A “Yes” vote will prohibit the City from selling, leasing, conveying, declaring surplus, or
permanently repurposing the Parking Plazas for any use other than surface parking without a
majority vote of the City’s voters.

A “No” vote will preserve the City’s discretion to use the Parking Plazas for any use permitted by
local, state, and/or federal law.

parking lots located in the Downtown area which are owned by the City.” They are commonly
known as Plazas | through 10.

The 2026 Ballot Measure Impact Analysis - 9212 Report (“9212 Report”) for Measure D found that
“’,. the Ballot Measure would potentially limit new development by adding additional constraints to
development on the City-owned Downtown Parking Plazas. Although there is an exception for
‘affordable housing’ on Plazas 7 and 8, it is not clear if mixed-income housing or other development
programs that include affordable housing could be approved without a subsequent Ballot Measure.
This would impact development of even affordable multifamily housing on all these lots, including
Plazas 7 and 8, by potentially complicating development opportunities. This would impact Program
1.H (‘Facilitation housing on City-owned sites’) and other Housing Element programs and policies.”

Unless approved by a majority vote of the City’s voters, Measure D would prohibit the City from
taking the following actions affecting the Parking Plazas: selling, leasing, or otherwise conveying
them; changing their use which would dimmish the availability of public parking; declaring them as
surplus land; constructing any capital project that permanently diminishes the availability of public
parking; modifying them by adding additional levels; modifying them in a way that would
negatively affect protected trees or tree canopy; or entering into a development agreement or similar
agreement that would allow a third-party to take action prohibited by it.

Measure D provides few actions to be taken without a majority vote of the City’s voters such as
maintaining and repairing the Parking Plazas and hosting the farmers’ market or similar short-term
events.

The processing, interpretation, and validity of Measure D would be governed by the Election Code
and state law. The 9212 Report found “If the Ballot Measure were to pass and then subsequently be
challenged in court, the City would be required to pay defense costs of the challenge and potentially
indemnify the proponents. The City would also be required to defend the Ballot Measure and any
implementation of the Ballot Measure, until ended by voters.” The 9212 Report attached the June
15, 2026, YIMBY Law letter that stated, “To dispel any potential ambiguity, we are prepared to sue
Los Altos the instant this measure is adopted.” Measure D’s defense costs would come from the

City’s General Fund.

A “Yes” vote will prohibit the City from selling, leasing, conveying, declaring surplus, or
permanently repurposing the Parking Plazas for any use other than surface parking without a
majority vote of the City’s voters.

A “No” vote will preserve the City’s discretion to use the Parking Plazas for any use permitted by
local, state, and/or federal law.

Section 21.04.010  Title 
This Chapter shall be known as the "Cupertino Parks and Open Space Protection 
Initiative." 
Section 21.04.020.  Purpose and Intent.  The purpose of this Chapter is as follows: 
A. 
To preserve lands designated as Parks and Open Space on the Cupertino 
General Plan Land Use Map. 
B. 
To reserve to the voters of the City of Cupertino the authority to approve 
any redesignation of such lands, or approval of development inconsistent with the Parks

only upon approval of at least two-thirds (2/3) of the voters of the City of Cupertino. 
Section 21.04.030.  Definitions. 
A.  
"Protected Parks and Open Space Land" means those parcels and portions

designated as "Parks and Open Space" on the Land Use Map of the Cupertino General 
Plan on the effective date of this Chapter. 
 
  
B. 
"Non-Park Use" means any use, development, or land use designation other 
than Parks and Open Space as shown on the City of Cupertino Land Use Map, including 
any successor or substantially similar land use designation, that would allow residential, 
commercial, industrial or mixed-use development containing residential, commercial or 
industrial uses on Protected Parks and Open Space Land.

General Plan Redesignation. 
No amendment to the Cupertino General Plan may redesignate Protected Parks and
